clue.text: Sell what's essential to 'salsa' here

indicators.note: what is essential to a phrase is its core, so only the inner part of the spelt-out grid reference is kept

parts.note: SALSA is the answer at 7 down, so where it sits in this grid is spelt out as the words seven down

explanation.surface: A street trader is told what must go into a salsa sold on this stall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salsa' points to the grid: SALSA is the answer at 7 down. Write that as SEVEN DOWN and drop the outer letters SE and OWN to keep the core, VEND.
explanation.definitionFit: To vend is to offer goods for sale, as a vending machine does.

clue.text: Unfortunately no use fixating 6 with green eyes

indicators.note: fixating means fastening something in place, here holding a piece inside the jumbled letters
something gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters of no use are jumbled

parts.note: 6 in Roman numerals is VI

explanation.surface: Someone jealous fixes their stare on a rival, to no avail.
explanation.walkthrough: '6' looks like a cross-reference to another answer, but here it is just the number, VI in Roman numerals. 'fixating' puts VI inside ENOUS, the anagram of NO USE.
explanation.definitionFit: Jealousy is the green-eyed monster in Othello, so someone with green eyes is jealous of another.

clue.text: Force Northern Irish to enter service

indicators.note: to enter means the following pieces go inside the word for force

parts.note: dint means force, as in the phrase by dint of
Erse is an old name for the Irish Gaelic language

explanation.surface: Northern Irish recruits are pressed into military service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' looks military in the surface, but it means a set of plates and dishes. DINT survives mainly in the phrase 'by dint of', meaning by force of.
explanation.definitionFit: A service is a matching set of crockery, such as a tea service or a set for dining.

clue.text: Is taciturn" different from scientific"?

indicators.note: different means made into something else, so the letters of is taciturn are rearranged

explanation.surface: A quiz question asks whether keeping silent counts as something other than scientific.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link word. The question mark admits the definition is loose: someone with a scientific rather than an arty turn of mind could be called lacking in art.
explanation.definitionFit: The arts and the sciences are traditional opposites, so a scientific bent is cast here as the lack of an aesthetic one.

clue.text: Our generation's latent desire?

indicators.note: latent means present but not on show, so the letters sit unseen inside the words our generation

explanation.surface: A commentator wonders what our age secretly longs for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'latent' signals the run hidden across 'Our generation'; the 's is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An urge is a strong want or impulse, the same as a desire.

clue.text: As 13 and 6 do to imitate "Starboard" and "Port" here?

definitions.text: As 13 and 6 do to imitate "Starboard" and "Port" here?

parts.words: As 13 and 6 do to imitate "Starboard" and "Port" here?
parts.note: the two quarrelsome twins at 13 and 6 in Through the Looking-Glass settle on having a battle; starboard and port are the opposite sides of a ship, set against each other in the grid

explanation.surface: Two famous twins mimic the two sides of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedledum and Tweedledee agree to fight, which is a settled disagreement; starboard (right) and port (left) are opposite sides that keep apart.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to accept a difference of opinion without further argument, a truce such as the twins strike before their battle.

clue.text: River took cummings to alleged spoiler

parts.note: the Tweed is a river on the border of Scotland and England
led means took, as in took someone by the hand
the poet e e cummings signed his name with lower-case initials, E E

explanation.surface: A river carried the poet cummings off to a supposed vandal.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass Tweedledum accuses his twin of spoiling his nice new rattle, hence the alleged spoiler.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lewis Carroll's book one twin is accused by his brother of ruining a new rattle, so he is the accused wrecker.

clue.text: Steps taken to make hot sauce

definitions.meaning: a lively Latin American dance, a set of steps

explanation.surface: Dance steps are used to whip up a spicy sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a Latin dance and a piquant Mexican relish, two unrelated senses.

clue.text: Nervously Ringo's up informed the other Beatles?

indicators.note: nervously suggests twitching and agitation, so the letters of Ringo are scrambled

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A jittery Ringo, out of bed, briefs his three bandmates.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text 'S N P' is an OCR garble of ''s up'. 'informed' is a link word; the question mark marks the definition as a playful example. 'Nervously' turns RINGO into INGRO.
explanation.definitionFit: A clique of insiders is a tight exclusive set, which the other three Beatles could be seen as, with Ringo the late arrival.

clue.text: Original No I for Arsenal granted a game playing up front

indicators.note: up front means placed ahead, so the versus letter comes before the jumbled letters
No I stands for number one, the first in line, so only the opening letter of Arsenal is taken

parts.note: a team playing another is shown as V, for versus, in fixture lists

indicators.note: game here means ready for anything, a loose signal that the letters of granted a are reworked

explanation.surface: A new signing at Arsenal is handed a match as a striker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up front' reads as a striker's position, but it puts V ahead of ANTGARDE, the anagram of GRANTED A signalled by 'game'. 'No I' is the newspaper's No 1.
explanation.definitionFit: Avant-garde art is new and experimental, so it is original in the sense of innovative.

clue.text: Toy I left in van

indicators.note: in van means at the front, as the van leads a procession, so the letter for left comes first

parts.note: ego is Latin for I, and means the self

explanation.surface: A child's plaything has been abandoned in a delivery van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'van' looks like a vehicle but means the vanguard: 'in van' puts L at the front of EGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Lego is a well-known plastic building-brick toy from Denmark.

clue.text: Writer taken in by Australian animal lover

indicators.note: taken in by means held inside the following word, so the writer's piece sits within the animal

parts.note: roo is short for kangaroo, the Australian animal
the writer of a clue refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: A writer is fooled by someone who adores Australian wildlife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'animal lover' reads as one phrase, but 'lover' alone is the definition. In crosswords the setter calls themself 'me', so 'Writer' gives ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's young man in love with Juliet gives his name to any ardent male sweetheart.

clue.text: Writer playing TV role as chief?

parts.note: a pen is a writing implement, so a writer
the dragons are the investors on the BBC TV show Dragons' Den

explanation.surface: An author is cast in a television part as the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' is a link word. The investors on the British TV show Dragons' Den are called dragons.
explanation.definitionFit: Pendragon was the title of an ancient British war leader, as in Uther Pendragon, father of King Arthur.

clue.text: Sentimental M muddle's done for N TIS N G one in battle

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'Sentimental M muddle's done for N TIS N G one in battle': TWEE plus ana of MUDDLE gives the answer, but 'M' and 'N TIS N G' are OCR garble and no scan or blog gives the printed words
annotationWithheld.clue: Sentimental M muddle's done for N TIS N G one in battle

clue.text: Reserve crew lives on and on?

indicators.note: on and on means repeated again, so the word for lives appears twice

parts.note: is means lives or exists, as in where there is life

explanation.surface: A spare rowing team carries on endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isis is the Oxford University reserve crew in the Boat Race, named after the stretch of the Thames at Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford's second eight in the Boat Race is named after the local name for the Thames, so it is the backup boat.

clue.text: Court works around depression for Spotty Dog's owners

indicators.note: around means the first pieces surround the one for depression

parts.note: to woo is to court a sweetheart
ops is short for opera, the plural of opus, meaning works
a dent is a small hollow or depression

explanation.surface: A tennis court is laid out around a dip for a dog's owners.
explanation.walkthrough: The Woodentops was a 1950s British children's TV puppet show about a family whose pet was Spotty Dog. OPS is the plural of the abbreviation op, for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: The puppet family in an old BBC children's programme kept a pet called Spotty Dog.

clue.text: Order to eat in includes confounded plonk!

indicators.note: includes means the jumbled letters hold another piece inside them
order means put into a new arrangement, so the letters of eat in are rearranged

parts.note: blew means botched or confounded, as in blew it

explanation.surface: An instruction to dine indoors brings a baffling cheap drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link word. 'Order' rearranges EAT IN into TAINE, and 'includes' puts BLEW inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Plonk is British slang for cheap everyday wine, the ordinary sort served with meals.

clue.text: He dealt poorly with kin, etc

indicators.note: poorly means badly done, so the letters of he dealt and kin are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man handled his relatives badly, and so on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link word joining the two parts of the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Etcetera means and other things of the same sort, which this phrase says in plain English.

clue.text: Pole sick at work with hammer?

parts.note: N stands for north, one of the earth's poles
ailing means sick or unwell

explanation.surface: A Polish worker feels ill while using a hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person, but it is the North Pole, N.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving in nails is what a hammer is used for, so someone busy with one is doing this.

clue.text: Bum a wine cask, as might Part I of …

definitions.meaning: a large barrel for wine or ale
the first part of the next answer is a billy goat, which charges with its head

explanation.surface: A tramp cadges a barrel of wine, like the first half of the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 21: the first word of that answer is BILLY, and a billy goat rams with its head.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means backside, a big cask, and to ram with the head as goats do, three unrelated senses.

clue.text: Do college principals articulate them?

parts.note: the basic principles of schooling are reading, writing and arithmetic, and the clue plays on whether heads pronounce those basics properly

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the heads of colleges speak clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principals' puns on principles: the three Rs are the basics of education, and only one of the three really begins with R when spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Reading, writing and arithmetic are the traditional foundations of elementary education.

clue.text: … novel rendition of Spooner's Man in the Flower Shop?

indicators.note: Spooner's signals that the opening sounds of two words are swapped, after the Reverend Spooner

parts.note: a man in a florist's could be a buyer of lilies
the customer in the florist's is the one who buys

explanation.surface: A novel take on a man shopping for flowers, as the Reverend Spooner might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: A LILY BUYER with its opening sounds swapped becomes BILLY LIAR, the 1959 novel by Keith Waterhouse. 'rendition of' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Keith Waterhouse wrote this book about a daydreaming Yorkshire undertaker's clerk, later filmed.

clue.text: 28 litres over, no less!

indicators.note: over means placed above in a down answer, so the letter for litres sits on top

parts.note: 28 refers to the answer at 28 across, the direction

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of having twenty-eight litres to spare, no less.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'over' means on top, so L goes above EAST, the answer at 28.
explanation.definitionFit: At the very least means no less than that, the minimum amount.

clue.text: A way to get over booze? Brandy bottles

indicators.note: bottles means holds inside, so the letters sit within the words booze brandy

explanation.surface: A drinker asks how to sober up, with brandy on the shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' looks like containers for the brandy, but it is the hidden-word signal. 'get over' reads as recovering from a hangover, but means crossing the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A striped pedestrian crossing in Britain is named after the animal, so it is a means of crossing a road.

clue.text: Stars only RADA admits

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so the letters sit inside the words only RADA

explanation.surface: Only the drama school takes on famous actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests actors at RADA, the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London, but it is a constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyra is a small northern constellation containing the bright star Vega.

clue.text: The other side of the radio from 11?

definitions.text: The other side of the radio from 11?

parts.words: The other side of the radio from 11?
parts.note: the answer at 11 is the radio alphabet word for R, right; the code word for its opposite, L for left, is wanted

explanation.surface: Someone asks what lies on the far side of a radio set.
explanation.walkthrough: In the NATO radio alphabet ROMEO stands for R and LIMA for L, so they stand for right and left, opposite sides.
explanation.definitionFit: The radio alphabet code word for L stands for left, the opposite side to right.

clue.text: Wash desirable, but you'd be ill-advised to air it!

definitions.text: Wash desirable, but you'd be ill-advised to air it!

parts.words: Wash desirable, but you'd be ill-advised to air it!
parts.note: the soiled sheets and clothes need washing, but the saying warns against airing private scandal in public

explanation.surface: Soiled laundry should be washed but not hung out where others can see.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'don't wash your dirty linen in public' means keep private scandals private.
explanation.definitionFit: Soiled bedclothes stand idiomatically for private embarrassing matters best kept from public view.

clue.text: What child's up on getting admitted to permeate unusual medium?

indicators.note: getting admitted to means let into, so the child's word goes inside the jumbled letters
unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters of permeate are rearranged

parts.note: a gee-gee is a child's word for a horse, abbreviated GG, which a child rides on

explanation.surface: Something a child stands on soaks through an odd painting material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges the fodder into EETEMPERA. GG, for gee-gee, is nursery talk for a horse, which is why a child is up on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg tempera is a paint in which pigment is bound with egg yolk, an artist's medium.

clue.text: Direction when taken in film

indicators.note: taken in means held inside, so the word for when goes within the film title

parts.note: E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film about an alien
as means when, as in as I left

explanation.surface: Instructions on when a film is to be shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction' looks like film direction, but it is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: East is one of the four cardinal points of the compass.
